network.tdh.formal.metadataDescription: TDH-v1 as a Lean 4 model: what it reproduces, what its proofs establish, what turned out to be false, and what the proofs do not cover.
network.tdh.formal.title: Formal model
network.tdh.formal.lede: TDH-v1 is also written as a mathematical model in Lean 4, a language in which a computer checks every step of every proof. The model runs, so it computes real days of TDH, and it carries proofs of the rule’s key properties. This page says what is proved, what was shown false, and what the proofs do not cover.
network.tdh.formal.status: A proposal, not yet adopted. The English specification, P26, stays the rule; the plan is for this model to become the normative reference for the computation.

By its PROOFS.md, round 4 starts from the raw Ethereum logs: it proves that their order cannot change the result, that the model on decoded inputs is its special case, and that a day with a result has every input value at its type, and it passes the 75 vectors of P26’s fourth round.
network.tdh.formal.why.title: Why write the rule again
network.tdh.formal.why.body: Plain English can be read more than one way. When a second implementation was written from the specification alone, it recorded 23 places where it had to make a choice. Two were rated high: whether N in the boost means the day number or the count of Memes, which give different boosts, and how to decode the delegation events at all, since P26 then gave no layouts. P26 now states a rule for each.
network.tdh.formal.why.body2: A formal model leaves no such room: every term has exactly one meaning, and the computer rejects a proof with a gap. Writing it paid off. It proved that the first version of D131’s netting rule could be changed by steps inside a transaction, in five cases, after the separately written program B found the flaw; P26’s uniform rule fixes all five. Its questions about P26 led to the clarifications of October 15, and its proofs showed which claims hold and which do not.
network.tdh.formal.featured.title: One theorem, read two ways
network.tdh.formal.featured.plain: Take two inputs whose transactions correspond one to one, in the same order: each pair shares one timestamp and one transaction hash, and moves the same net amount of every token for every address. If both replays succeed, with netting and the same consolidations, they leave every holding stack the same, for every token and every address.
network.tdh.formal.featured.means: So the order of a transaction’s steps, its round trips and its detours cannot change any holding stack.
network.tdh.formal.featured.limit: It stops there. Mint facts read the logged steps, so a mint and its burn inside one transaction leave every stack unchanged but can make a token eligible, giving a wallet a balance it did not have, and can change editions, rates and other holders’ TDH (counterexamples H and I below). A token’s balance and raw days stay the same while its eligibility does; that follows from P26 §7.2’s definitions and is not a theorem here. The underflow test also reads the steps, to decide whether an input is valid.
network.tdh.formal.featured.definitions: Its hypotheses, as defined in the model
network.tdh.formal.figure.title: Two inputs, one net movement
network.tdh.formal.figure.desc: Left: one transaction as logged, with three steps: A sends a copy to X, X sends it back, A sends a copy to B. Right: one transaction with one step, A sends a copy to B. Both move the same net amount for every address: A minus one, B plus one, X zero. Replayed with netting, both leave every holding stack the same.
network.tdh.formal.figure.resultNote: A keeps its other copies with their ages; B’s new copy starts at this transaction. Nothing is minted or burned, so no token’s eligibility changes, and balances and raw days are the same too.
network.tdh.formal.contains.title: What the model contains
network.tdh.formal.contains.body: The model covers P26 from canonical decoded inputs to the day’s records and totals, one module per part of the specification, including the input rules clarified on October 15 and a registry whose every field the rules read. Each definition quotes or cites its P26 section, and P26’s pseudocode sits next to the code that implements it. All arithmetic is on unbounded integers, so nothing can overflow or round by accident; the two binary64 roundings are emulated exactly.
network.tdh.formal.contains.bodyRaw: The model covers P26 from the raw Ethereum logs a node reads to the day’s records and totals, one module per part of the specification: which logs count, their positions, header order, decoding and the malformed-log rules, the type of every input value, and the input rules clarified on October 15, with a registry whose every field the rules read. Each definition quotes or cites its P26 section, and P26’s pseudocode sits next to the code that implements it. All arithmetic is on unbounded integers, so nothing can overflow or round by accident; the two binary64 roundings are emulated exactly.

The vector counts come from the proof manifest; the other runs are as the model’s README records them at {readme}.
network.tdh.formal.contains.runsRaw: The model runs. At its last build it passes all {vectors} of P26’s conformance vectors as of {spec} ({checks} checks); it reads all {rawLogs} logs of the October 11, 2026 cycle at their types and computes the cycle from them in {duration}, with the live total of {total} and all {records} wallet and identity records unchanged; and it matched the Python reference on {randomInputs} random inputs under both netting rules ({randomChecks} checks), about a third of them with some logs given raw. The vector counts come from the proof manifest; the other runs are as the model’s README records them at {readme}.
network.tdh.formal.contains.outside: Outside the model: selecting and decoding Ethereum logs, state reads and finality, the binding of the result header, and the legacy emulation. The vector runner has its own log decoder; it is test tooling, not part of the model.
network.tdh.formal.contains.outsideRaw: Outside the model: a node’s own reads (which chain is canonical and finalized, that its log set is complete, the headers it reads to find the snapshot block, and each Meme’s mint limit at that block), the vector runner’s JSON reader, the binding of the result header, and the legacy emulation. The rules for raw logs are definitions of the model: P26’s vectors, the whole day and the random inputs check that they say what P26 says; no theorem does.

network.tdh.formal.statements.title: What is proved, and what is not
network.tdh.formal.statements.intro: Every status below comes from the model’s proof manifest, which the build itself writes: a theorem counts as proved only when Lean’s kernel has checked it and it uses no axiom beyond Lean’s three standard ones. One statement holds by definition, P26’s stated numbers are checked by running the model, four claims turned out to be false, and one is not proved here. Open a row for its theorems and their axioms.

network.tdh.formal.st.netting.title: Netting invariance
network.tdh.formal.st.netting.plain: Every holding stack after the replay depends only on each transaction’s net movement of each token per address. Reordering a transaction’s transfers, or inserting a round trip anywhere in it, through a sink or not, changes no stack.
network.tdh.formal.st.netting.scope: Assumes that both replays succeed, that the two inputs’ transactions correspond one to one and in order, each pair sharing one timestamp and one transaction hash (P26 §3.2 requires it and the model checks it), and the same consolidations. Adding or removing a whole transaction, even one that moves nothing, is not covered, and the theorem starts from transfers already in canonical order. It is about the stacks only: mint facts read the logged steps, so eligibility, and with it a record’s balance and raw days, base, boost and final, can change (the next two rows).
network.tdh.formal.st.replay.title: The replay never fails
network.tdh.formal.st.replay.plain: Once the underflow test passes, the replay succeeds, with or without netting, and every stack outside the sinks holds exactly its address’s balance: what it received minus what it sent. That is why P26 need not test for underflow again in the replay.
network.tdh.formal.st.replay.scope: With netting, it also assumes P26’s transaction rules (one timestamp and transaction hash, net movements below 2^64). A sink’s stack is not a balance: sinks only receive.
network.tdh.formal.st.conservation.title: Copies are conserved
network.tdh.formal.st.conservation.plain: Summed over every address outside the sinks, the copies held of a token are the copies that came from a sink minus those that went to one. An address that never appears holds none.
network.tdh.formal.st.conservation.scope: The inflow counts transfers from the zero address (mints) and from 0x…dead, which creates copies (P26 §3.4). Holds for any registry’s sinks.
network.tdh.formal.st.identitySums.title: Identity sums
network.tdh.formal.st.identitySums.plain: In every day’s result, each identity’s balance, raw days and base TDH, in total and for every token, are the sums over exactly its wallet records, each counted once; and every wallet record belongs to exactly one identity.
network.tdh.formal.st.identitySums.scope: Not for boost and final, which are computed per record: see “Total = sum of wallets” below.
network.tdh.formal.st.order.title: Order independence
network.tdh.formal.st.order.plain: Reordering the decoded transfers, delegation events and ignored-log positions in any way gives the same result, or the same error, including the log-position checks of P26 §3.1. The order of the decoded items cannot matter.
network.tdh.formal.st.order.scope: A transfer’s position fields are part of the input: changing them changes the canonical order, as it should. Raw logs reach these lists through the decoder, which is outside the model, so the order of raw logs is not covered.
network.tdh.formal.st.orderRaw.title: Order independence, raw logs included
network.tdh.formal.st.orderRaw.plain: Reordering the raw logs, the decoded transfers and delegation events and the ignored-log positions, in any way, gives the same result, or no result for both, including the position checks of P26 §3.1 and the type checks of §3.2. The order of the raw logs and of the decoded items cannot change the result.
network.tdh.formal.st.orderRaw.scope: When several raw logs are malformed, which one the error names can depend on their order, so the theorem compares results, not error messages. A transfer’s position fields are part of the input: changing them changes the canonical order, as it should.
network.tdh.formal.st.rawLogs.title: The model from raw logs
network.tdh.formal.st.rawLogs.plain: The model on decoded inputs is the model on raw logs when no log is given raw, so every theorem above about decoded inputs holds there. And a day with a result has every input value at its type: the registry, the snapshot block and time, every transfer, delegation event and log position, every raw log and every header timestamp.
network.tdh.formal.st.rawLogs.scope: The rules for raw logs (which logs count, decoding, positions, header order and types) are definitions, not theorems: P26’s vectors, the October 11 cycle and random inputs check that they say what P26 says. The vector runner’s JSON reader is test tooling and is not proved.
network.tdh.formal.st.lifo.title: Last in, first out
network.tdh.formal.st.lifo.plain: The model’s compact stack is exactly P26’s ordered list: a purchase appends, a send removes exactly the last n entries in order and fails exactly when there are fewer, and its size is its length.
network.tdh.formal.st.lifo.scope: About how the model stores a stack: it behaves as P26’s list. Which entries the replay pushes and takes is covered by the rows above.
network.tdh.formal.st.totals.title: Totals
network.tdh.formal.st.totals.plain: The network total is the sum of identity finals, the total without sinks leaves out exactly the sink identities, the base and raw totals are sums too, and the total is below 2^53.
network.tdh.formal.st.totals.scope: This restates how the totals are defined; only the range check adds anything. A sum over wallets is a different number: see “Total = sum of wallets”.
network.tdh.formal.st.facts.title: P26’s stated numbers
network.tdh.formal.st.facts.plain: The registry hash, the half-cent rate ties for H = 3,941, BASE’s rounding, ADD(2) = 50,000, ADD(3) = 82,645, ADD(n) = 144,051 from 33 sets, no ties in the boost’s rounding, the final ties that round down, removal from the end of a stack, and the positions of ignored logs.
network.tdh.formal.st.facts.scope: Evaluated at every build, which trusts Lean’s compiler; not proved in the kernel.
network.tdh.formal.st.facts.count: {checks} checks in Tdh/Facts.lean, evaluated at every build.
network.tdh.formal.st.factsTyped.title: P26’s stated numbers
network.tdh.formal.st.factsTyped.plain: The registry hash, the half-cent rate ties for H = 3,941, BASE’s rounding, ADD(2) = 50,000, ADD(3) = 82,645, ADD(n) = 144,051 from 33 sets, no ties in the boost’s rounding, the final ties that round down, removal from the end of a stack, and the positions of ignored logs. Since round 4 also the rule identifier, the types of values (the registry’s, and the full range of 256-bit and signed 64-bit values), which dates are cycle dates, the highest block a cutoff can have, and that a log is given raw or decoded, never both.
network.tdh.formal.st.factsTyped.scope: Evaluated at every build, which trusts Lean’s compiler; not proved in the kernel.
network.tdh.formal.st.beyondStacks.title: Steps inside a transaction never matter
network.tdh.formal.st.beyondStacks.plain: False beyond the stacks. Inserting a mint of 10 copies and its burn into one transaction leaves every stack unchanged, but 10 more copies count as minted: the largest edition doubles, another card’s rate doubles from 2.00 to 4.00, and another holder’s final doubles from 800 to 1,600. A mint and its burn can also make a token eligible: a wallet with no record gets a balance of 5, and another holder goes from 32 to 60.
network.tdh.formal.st.beyondStacks.scope: Counterexamples H and I, checked at every build. Since October 15, P26 §7.1 states the property for the stacks only. Whether such mints should count toward editions is flagged for the owner, not decided.
network.tdh.formal.st.balanceRaw.title: Balances and raw days, when eligibility is unchanged
network.tdh.formal.st.balanceRaw.plain: For every token whose eligibility the steps leave as it was, a record’s balance and raw days stay the same too: both are read from the token’s stacks and the cutoff time.
network.tdh.formal.st.balanceRaw.scope: This follows from P26 §7.2’s definitions, and P26 says so; the model does not prove it as a theorem.
network.tdh.formal.st.minted.title: Held = minted − burned
network.tdh.formal.st.minted.plain: False. A transfer from 0x…dead credits its recipient with a fresh copy and is not a mint. Case G: one copy minted, one sent by 0x…dead, two held. What holds instead is the conservation law above.
network.tdh.formal.st.minted.scope: Proved false with a counterexample the build checks.
network.tdh.formal.st.walletSum.title: Total = sum of wallets
network.tdh.formal.st.walletSum.plain: False. Each record’s boost is computed on its own holdings. Case F: two wallets of one identity each hold one Gradient for 100 days; each wallet record has boost 1.02 and final 102, and the identity has boost 1.04 and final 208. The total is 208, not 204.
network.tdh.formal.st.walletSum.scope: P26 §7.3 now says so, with this example. A page that adds up wallet values will not match the total.
network.tdh.formal.st.firstRule.title: The first netting rule
network.tdh.formal.st.firstRule.plain: False: under D131’s first rule, steps inside a transaction could change even the holding stacks. Five cases are proved in the kernel; the uniform rule P26 adopted the same day gives equal results in each.
network.tdh.formal.st.firstRule.scope: Totals from the model, first rule against the current one.
network.tdh.formal.st.cap.title: The 19.99% cap
network.tdh.formal.st.cap.plain: With at least six parties of positive weight, no party, capped or not, counts more than 19.99% of the counted total, and the key slices add up exactly. For the live roster it holds for the registered weight W with no assumption on keys, because an account is live only while it keeps a valid key. The loop stops within six passes.
network.tdh.formal.st.cap.scope: A separate small model of the cap. Each account’s keys after the no-pool rule, the lease and group membership are inputs, not proved; with fewer than six parties of positive weight there is no cap and the theorems say nothing.
network.tdh.formal.st.exclusions.title: Exclusions
network.tdh.formal.st.exclusions.plain: For a node that keeps incident records, each with its step and length fixed when it opens, as P53 §13.1 now prescribes: no evidence shortens an exclusion in force, exclusions never overlap, stretch or repeat, and pruning old records on P53’s schedule changes no exclusion.
network.tdh.formal.st.exclusions.scope: For a node that recomputes incidents from the evidence it still holds, the claim is false: an exclusion can end 298 cycles early. P53 now rules recomputation out.

network.tdh.formal.not.title: What the proofs do not guarantee
network.tdh.formal.not.english.title: That the English text says the same thing.
network.tdh.formal.not.english.body: People check that the model matches the specification; a disagreement is fixed in one or the other and recorded. On October 15, P26 settled the ten questions the model had raised, and in later rounds the findings of the four-way differential tests and their reviews. P26’s fifth round, on October 16, settled the questions the model’s fourth round had left, among them that decoded transfers at one log position share one contract, sender and recipient; the model has yet to follow it. Flagged for the owner and still open: whether mints inside a transaction should count toward editions.
network.tdh.formal.not.programs.title: That the programs match the model on every input.
network.tdh.formal.not.programs.body: At the model’s build, the model and both references in the design repository, in Python and in Rust, passed the same {vectors} vectors, and the model matched the Python reference on a whole real day and on 6,000 random inputs. Four rounds of differential tests on October 15 ran generated cycles through the model, the Python reference, the Rust core and program B. The first, 40,000 cycles, agreed on every value and differed only on whether 20 inputs were valid. The second, 35,000 cases after P26’s clarifications, found six more problems: which inputs are valid, three registry lists the Rust core could not read, 54 cases where Python formed other clusters, an event’s default use case and logs marked removed. The third, 35,000 cases on P26’s third round, found the model, the Python reference and program B equal on all 30,000 main cases, two faults the Rust core had copied from the Rust reference, and two more input rules. P26 settled those findings the same day. The fourth, 35,000 cases on P26’s fourth round and the model’s round 4, found the model and program B equal on all 30,000 main cases, and two defects in how the Rust core and the Python reference read the vector files (F8, F9), which P26’s fifth round settled on October 16. The references follow P26’s fifth round; the Rust core and program B, in the validator’s current code, its fourth. Tests can miss cases: no machine-checked proof links any program’s code to the model.
network.tdh.formal.not.inputs.title: That the inputs are right.
network.tdh.formal.not.inputs.body: Selecting and decoding Ethereum logs, state reads and finality are outside the model. Validators are to check every block’s events against Ethereum’s block headers (D118), and two separately written programs are being built to prove each day’s result from Ethereum’s history (D119).
network.tdh.formal.not.inputs.bodyRaw: A node’s own reads are outside the model: which chain is canonical and finalized, that its log set is complete, the headers it reads to find the snapshot block, and each Meme’s mint limit at that block. The rules that select and decode logs are definitions of the model, checked by vectors and runs, not proved. Validators are to check every block’s events against Ethereum’s block headers (D118), and two separately written programs are being built to prove each day’s result from Ethereum’s history (D119).
network.tdh.formal.not.rule.title: That the rule is the right rule.
network.tdh.formal.not.rule.body: A proof shows the rule does what it says, not that it is fair or wise. Rule changes are owner decisions.
network.tdh.formal.not.lean.title: Lean itself.
network.tdh.formal.not.lean.body: The proofs rely on Lean’s small kernel and its three standard axioms, which the build audits for every theorem and the manifest lists theorem by theorem. The {facts} checks of P26’s stated facts and some counterexamples are evaluations that also trust Lean’s compiler.
network.tdh.formal.layers.title: Three layers of assurance
network.tdh.formal.layers.desc: The English specification is checked against the Lean model by people. Inside the Lean model, the proofs are the only machine-checked links. The model and the programs pass the same conformance vectors, the model was compared with the Python reference on a whole day and on 6,000 random inputs, and all four were run on generated cycles in four rounds of differential tests. The programs check each other: Rust and Python in the daily comparison, and Rust and program B inside every validator once it runs both. Inputs are checked separately.
network.tdh.formal.layers.programsSub: Rust core, program B, Python reference
network.tdh.formal.layers.vectors: Shared conformance vectors; a whole day and 6,000 random inputs against Python; four rounds of generated cycles across four programs
network.tdh.formal.layers.inputsBody: Checked reads (D118) and proofs A and B (D119), outside the model
network.tdh.formal.layers.machine: Machine-checked: the proofs inside the Lean model
network.tdh.formal.layers.human: Checked by people or by tests
network.tdh.formal.check.title: How you will be able to check
network.tdh.formal.check.body: The model lives in 6529’s design repository, beside the specification and its vectors. Once that source is published, anyone with Lean installed can rebuild it, which re-checks every proof and audits its axioms, and run the vectors through it:
network.tdh.formal.check.commands:
lake build
lake exe tdh-vectors ../tdh-reference/vectors   # {passed} of {total}, {checks} checks
lake exe tdh-vectors vectors-netting           # {nettingPassed} of {nettingTotal}
python3 tools/manifest.py                      # the manifest this page reads
